Cabin Pressure

By: Bernadette Maguire | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Exclusive footage inside the cabin on Sunday night as a Safair flight experienced a loss of cabin pressure forcing the plane to drop 20000 feet in a matter of minutes.

Summary:
We have 38 minutes of footage exclusive to us until after the show on Sunday night - shot by sports cameraman on board the SAfair flight from Johannesburg to Cape Town on Sunday night.

About an hour into the flight the plane lost cabin pressure and the oxygen masks were manually dropped for the passengers. Some passengers in the footage reported that the masks did not work.

Passengers panicked and say that communucation was scant and the airlines handling of the situation was terrible.

Couple that with the fact that not only did the same airline have a problem 48 hours before with the same issue - it was the third incident of its kind in less than 8 months.

It's brought maintenance and safety into question. Fortunately in all three instances the pilots handled the situations perfectly to avoid catastrophe.

Cabin pressure is always carefully controlled and air disasters like the Helios plane crash in 2005 are largley due to pilot error. A small jet went down at the end of last year in Caledon killing the pilot due to a pressurisation issue. So its not commonplace but it does happen.

What causes it and how should you react? And what are Safair doing to ensure their flights are safe?

3) Say positive about him saving the day despite the problem there was no accident, and show his photo. He aviated, navigated and communicated – make that quite clear
4) They also say no rapid descent.
5) Story is not to harm them, it’s about an incident that occurred where a pilot saved the day. Lets hear from Carl Jensen more and use him better about the pilot doing well.
6) Make it clear that it happened over Bloem
7) At the oxygen masks: Bring up everything they say in response on screen – bring in all they say about the oxygen masks not actually being required, they were only for comfort and never required that was why they were dropped manually and also that they dont blow in your face and all of them were working. Take it verbatim. As an additional precaution the pilot decided to release the oxygen masks manually to comfort and reassure the passengers ... etc
8) Say VOICE OF CABIN CREW where they talk in the footage
9) Bring in Guy Leech saying they really did well and saved the day up MUCH earlier
10) And bring in earlier that its safer to fly and script: your chances of dying are not is
11) Take out the passenger saying he would prefer to drive.
12) Spelling error in sub title – drastic – please triple check them all we will not have time to fix them.
13) LOSE HELIOS

4) Include their comments on the East London flight
5) They do their own maintenance – did we ever ask them about maintenance? We need to be 100% clear cause the way Guy Leech talks about their maintenance sounded derogatory.

Press Release:


Cabin Pressure
Imagine you’re an hour into your flight when the cabin suddenly loses pressure, oxygen masks are manually deployed and the pilot forces the plane to steadily descend. Why did this happen on two recent SAFAIR flights between Johannesburg and Cape Town? It’s the third incident of this kind in just nine months and has brought maintenance and safety into question. Carte Blanche shares passengers’ experiences through exclusive, on-board footage.


Script:


The Civil Aviation AuScript – Cabin Pressure

VO:
There was much jubilation on SAfair flight FA103 on Sunday night. This time it wasn’t just for a smooth landing. (upsound) Captain Lawrence Banda and first officer Charles Peck saved the day in the eyes of the 265 passengers on board. After an unexpected decompression event in airspace over Bloemfontein they turned the plane around bringing everyone on board back to safety on a scheduled Joburg to Cape Town flight.

Upsound:
The pilots did their best.
Thank you for landing us!


VO:
Filmmakers Joshua Rowe and Brett Cox filmed the entire event which they say started with a loud bang.

Brett:
We suddenly heard a noise on the wing

Joshua:
I immediately thought well I wonder what that is, I wonder if they are going to make an announcement and tell us if there is something wrong with the plane?

Brett
We looked at each other, like what was that and then kind of just shrugged it off.

VO: 5”
Then just a few minutes later oxygen masks were released from the ceiling.

Brett:
A little bit of panic everywhere you are kind of just processing why have the gas masks dropped?

VO: 4”
That’s when he started filming.

Brett:
Initially it was just because it was something exciting. Then the fear set in and then it became I am not filming this for the exciting factor, maybe this could be looked at if something goes wrong.

Joshua:
You never know what happens, you never know what can go wrong – or if that will be the only footage from the flight.

Joshua:
We are now waiting to hear what’s happening.

Josh:
Soon after that an announcement was made that we would be descending rapidly and we would need to brace and put our seatbelts on and those kind of things.

VO: 9”
They say that a mixture of fear and confusion reigned on the plane. Some of the passengers said their masks were not working.

Upsound
Is yours working?

Brett: The lady in front of me with her son, she started to panic because her oxygen wasn’t coming out and she looked back at me with big eyes and I gave her my mask. She took that one and I took her one and then I was like what is going on here?

John:
So it wasn’t working?

Brett:
No I couldn’t feel any air coming out or anything so then I started to have a panic.


VO:
The plane they later heard had suffered a gradual loss of cabin pressure and the pilot had released the masks as a precautionary measure. The second incident of its kind last weekend. In a written reply to us Safair said “All masks on the two flights last weekend were operating and the oxygen system was operating properly. The fact that the passengers could not feel the oxygen flow is perfectly normal and does not mean the oxygen does not work.”

This was confirmed by retired SAA captain Karl Jensen.

Karl:
The oxygen bag doesn’t inflate it’s a mixed system where it takes ambient air and oxygen. So it doesn’t blow up into a balloon.

VO:3:
Here’s how pressurization works.

Karl:
The air comes from the engines they call it bleed air. So its compressed air from the engines that comes in through a heat exchanger and it cools it down through a system called an air conditioning pack. That air comes out as conditioned air and that pressurizes the aircraft. Now if you keep pumping the air in it will blow up like a balloon. So you have got an outflow valve that regulates the pressure inside the aircraft and that outflow valve is a very sensitive device.

VO: 10
A loss of cabin pressure is rare but it does happen and crew are trained to deal with it. Is a bit like a puncture in a car tyre says aviation editor Guy Leitch.

Guy:
This was more like a slow leak, the tyre was going flat slowly and again you want to get off the road or you want to get back so you can fix the problem as quickly as possible but it wasn’t in this case life threatening because the key thing is the crew had identified it in time.

VO: 9”
If only cabin crew had explained this perhaps some passengers would not have been so anxious.

Joshua:
And I think that caused a lot of confusion in people and kids starting crying because they were probably just freaked out.

Upsound:
Sorry, sorry can you tell us what’s happening here?

Cabin crew
I, I haven’t. I can’t even contact the flight crew and let me know how. They told us resume our duties so its not umm, a drastic situation.

VO: 6”
And when the cabin crew finally addressed the passengers over the intercom they didn’t exactly instill a sense of calm says Brett.

Brett:
You could hear in the voice on the intercom, initially a shaky voice, a big sigh.

VO: 7
Which is why it’s so important for the cabin crew to keep passengers reassured.

Guy:
They are not just trolley dollies they are not just waitresses, they actually fulfill a very important safety function.

VO: 9
Its difficult for the pilot to communicate to the passengers during this kind of incident as they need to follow what’s called the ANC mantra.

Karl:
Aviate Navigate Communicate. To aviate is to fly the airplane, whether its on autoflight, yourself. Navigate to make sure you are not going to bump into anyone or mountains and things like that. And then communicate.

VO:
The pilot dropped the plane from 32000 to 10 000 feet in 8 minutes.

Brett:
My left ear just would not equalize and I was in a lot of stress and pain.

VO: 9”
A fairly rapid descent to a level where the passengers can breathe normally around 10 000 feet is needed because there is limited oxygen on board.

Karl:
You only have enough oxygen in the system to get you down to a safe level otherwise you are carrying great big tanks of oxygen that never get used.

Upsound
We require your full co-operation. We will be making a precautionary emergency landing on land in approximately nine minutes.

Brett:
And I then was…Wow this has just become very, very real. We are actually going to drop on a farm or a field and I was just thinking this isstraight out of some movie.

Vo: 13”
Safair maintain their crew were calm and professional. They
explained that the crew saying that they were landing on land comes directly from the Civil aviation safety manual and is meant to clarify that they are landing on land as opposed to water. Brett feels a more specific explanation in laymans terms may have prevented panic that night. The pilot, however played it by the book.

John Link
The incident over Bloemfontein was the third involving a Safair flight in the space of 9 months. In each instance there was a pressurization issue.

VO: 27”
On Friday 22nd of January, Safair suffered a loss of cabin pressure – on the same plane along the same route. And just 9 months prior passenger Mariette Rossouw posted this footage on a Cape Town to Port Elizabeth flight which also suffered a loss of cabin pressure. The Civil Aviation Authority confirmed that in that instance it was a different plane.

Guy:
It’s extraordinary bad luck to have two depressurization incidents on the same aircraft in immediately sequential flights. It defies belief.

VO: 20”
Safair confirmed that they had resolved the problem and CEO Elmar Conradie apologized for any inconvenience caused saying they appreciate and understand that some passethority’s Simon Segwabe has the series of incidents on his radar.

Simon:
It is a quite serious issue in that if the aircraft flies at that altitude and loses pressurization , the difficulty that the passenger will have in terms of breathing.
It is a safety concern to us.

VO: 6
They have since grounded the plane pending the outcome of their investigation.

John link:
We’ve been told by an industry insider that this particular aircraft suffers from what is known as intermittent snags.

VO: 21
According to our source the same plane had suffered a decompression event just days before last weekend’s events. In this instance one of the planes 2 aircon packs which form part of the pressurization units allegedly failed on an East London route forcing the pilot to fly at 25000 feet.

VO: 7”
Safair admitted that one of the aircons needed to be reset on the ground on the 18th of January just 4 days before the first incident. “The aircraft returned to the bay and the system was reset and declared “operationally normal.” The snag that resulted in the trip had absolutely nothing to do with the pressurization system.”

Guy:
There are too many coincidences going here to be comfortable with. It’s so unlikely that the same aircraft would have two separate pressurization issues for apparently different reasons. The chances of that are very unlikely. It does mean that the civil aviation authority needs to step in here and do a fresh set of inspections.

John:
So where to from here in terms of the CAA and Safair?

Simon:
The aircraft is going through maintenance and to look at what are the other possibilities. Until a defect is found and tested to optimal the aircraft canno be back in service and Safair is aware of that.

Link
For most of us an airplane is an alien environment about which we understand very little. The incidents of the past few days have left a lot of people spooked. So the question is how safe is flying?

VO: 3
In reality your chances of dying in a airplane crash is one in a million.

Guy Leith:
It is safer to fly than it is to drive to and fro from the airport.

VO: 12”
Safair this week reassured passengers of their excellent safety record spanning 50 years. (PAUSE)

A record that they kept last Sunday.

Upsound
We are now returning back to Joburg. The situation is under control. We will be able to make a safe landing.

Brett
As when we landed the girl next to me grabbed my hand and was squeezing my hand…

VO: 5
The bus ride back to the terminal was abuzz with conversations.

Upsound.
You still filming!!! Hey we made it bro!

Brett
There was that initial we’re all a unit – we made it together.

VO:
It’s now incumbent on the CAA to go through voice recordings and interview crew as part of their investigation.

John:
When the report comes out will it be made public?

Simon
Yes. Our report gets released to the public.

John:
To satisfy ourselves the problem has been resolved.

Simon:
Definitely the problem has been resolved.

John:
And before that happens would you be comfortable to fly SAfair?

Simon:
I will fly safari I will fly any our airlines on any given day.

Karl:
You may have every confidence in the levels of safety of airlines operated in South Africa. The training the regulation of the maintenance that’s all absolutely dead right.

Promo 1:

VO: 10”
A pilot saved the day last Sunday on a Safair flight that suffered a gradual decompression over airspace in Bloemfontein. This time the passengers weren’t just clapping for a safe landing.
Clapping

Upsound
“The pilots did their best”


Promo 2:

VO: 8
What happens during a decompression event at 32000ft – we bring you exclusive footage taken during a safair flight last Sunday.

It’s not working?

VO: 4”
As long as your pilot knows what he’s doing it seems you are in safe hands.

Promo 3 10 seconds

2 decompression incidents involving the same safair plane last weekend have left the it grounded. We bring you exclusive footage of the incident and take you through the motions.

So its compressed air from the engines that comes in through a heat exchanger and it cools it down through a system called an air conditioning pack. That air comes out as conditioned air and that pressurizes the aircraft. Now if you keep pumping the air in it will blow up like a balloon. So you have got an outflow valve that regulates the pressure inside the aircraft and that outflow valve is a very sensitive device. VO: 10 A loss of cabin pressure is rare but it does happen and crew are trained to deal with it. Is a bit like a puncture in a car tyre says aviation editor Guy Leitch. Guy: This was more like a slow leak, the tyre was going flat slowly and again you want to get off the road or you want to get back so you can fix the problem as quickly as possible but it wasn’t in this case life threatening because the key thing is the crew had identified it in time. VO: 9” If only cabin crew had explained this perhaps some passengers would not have been so anxious. Joshua: And I think that caused a lot of confusion in people and kids starting crying because they were probably just freaked out. Upsound: Sorry, sorry can you tell us what’s happening here? Cabin crew I, I haven’t. I can’t even contact the flight crew and let me know how. They told us resume our duties so its not umm, a drastic situation. VO: 6” And when the cabin crew finally addressed the passengers over the intercom they didn’t exactly instill a sense of calm says Brett. Brett: You could hear in the voice on the intercom, initially a shaky voice, a big sigh. VO: 7 Which is why it’s so important for the cabin crew to keep passengers reassured. Guy: They are not just trolley dollies they are not just waitresses, they actually fulfill a very important safety function. VO: 9 Its difficult for the pilot to communicate to the passengers during this kind of incident as they need to follow what’s called the ANC mantra. Karl: Aviate Navigate Communicate. To aviate is to fly the airplane, whether its on autoflight, yourself. Navigate to make sure you are not going to bump into anyone or mountains and things like that. And then communicate. VO: The pilot dropped the plane from 32000 to 10 000 feet in 8 minutes. Brett: My left ear just would not equalize and I was in a lot of stress and pain. VO: 9” A fairly rapid descent to a level where the passengers can breathe normally around 10 000 feet is needed because there is limited oxygen on board. Karl: You only have enough oxygen in the system to get you down to a safe level otherwise you are carrying great big tanks of oxygen that never get used. Upsound We require your full co-operation. We will be making a precautionary emergency landing on land in approximately nine minutes. Brett: And I then was…Wow this has just become very, very real. We are actually going to drop on a farm or a field and I was just thinking this isstraight out of some movie. Vo: 13” Safair maintain their crew were calm and professional. They explained that the crew saying that they were landing on land comes directly from the Civil aviation safety manual and is meant to clarify that they are landing on land as opposed to water. Brett feels a more specific explanation in laymans terms may have prevented panic that night. The pilot, however played it by the book. John Link The incident over Bloemfontein was the third involving a Safair flight in the space of 9 months. In each instance there was a pressurization issue. VO: 27” On Friday 22nd of January, Safair suffered a loss of cabin pressure – on the same plane along the same route. And just 9 months prior passenger Mariette Rossouw posted this footage on a Cape Town to Port Elizabeth flight which also suffered a loss of cabin pressure. The Civil Aviation Authority confirmed that in that instance it was a different plane. Guy: It’s extraordinary bad luck to have two depressurization incidents on the same aircraft in immediately sequential flights. It defies belief. VO: 20” Safair confirmed that they had resolved the problem and CEO Elmar Conradie apologized for any inconvenience caused saying they appreciate and understand that some passethority’s Simon Segwabe has the series of incidents on his radar. Simon: It is a quite serious issue in that if the aircraft flies at that altitude and loses pressurization , the difficulty that the passenger will have in terms of breathing. It is a safety concern to us. VO: 6 They have since grounded the plane pending the outcome of their investigation. John link: We’ve been told by an industry insider that this particular aircraft suffers from what is known as intermittent snags. VO: 21 According to our source the same plane had suffered a decompression event just days before last weekend’s events. In this instance one of the planes 2 aircon packs which form part of the pressurization units allegedly failed on an East London route forcing the pilot to fly at 25000 feet. VO: 7” Safair admitted that one of the aircons needed to be reset on the ground on the 18th of January just 4 days before the first incident. “The aircraft returned to the bay and the system was reset and declared “operationally normal.” The snag that resulted in the trip had absolutely nothing to do with the pressurization system.” Guy: There are too many coincidences going here to be comfortable with. It’s so unlikely that the same aircraft would have two separate pressurization issues for apparently different reasons. The chances of that are very unlikely. It does mean that the civil aviation authority needs to step in here and do a fresh set of inspections. John: So where to from here in terms of the CAA and Safair? Simon: The aircraft is going through maintenance and to look at what are the other possibilities. Until a defect is found and tested to optimal the aircraft canno be back in service and Safair is aware of that. Link For most of us an airplane is an alien environment about which we understand very little. The incidents of the past few days have left a lot of people spooked. So the question is how safe is flying? VO: 3 In reality your chances of dying in a airplane crash is one in a million. Guy Leith: It is safer to fly than it is to drive to and fro from the airport. VO: 12” Safair this week reassured passengers of their excellent safety record spanning 50 years. (PAUSE) A record that they kept last Sunday. Upsound We are now returning back to Joburg. The situation is under control. We will be able to make a safe landing. Brett As when we landed the girl next to me grabbed my hand and was squeezing my hand… VO: 5 The bus ride back to the terminal was abuzz with conversations. Upsound. You still filming!!! Hey we made it bro! Brett There was that initial we’re all a unit – we made it together. VO: It’s now incumbent on the CAA to go through voice recordings and interview crew as part of their investigation. John: When the report comes out will it be made public? Simon Yes. Our report gets released to the public. John: To satisfy ourselves the problem has been resolved. Simon: Definitely the problem has been resolved. John: And before that happens would you be comfortable to fly SAfair? Simon: I will fly safari I will fly any our airlines on any given day. Karl: You may have every confidence in the levels of safety of airlines operated in South Africa. The training the regulation of the maintenance that’s all absolutely dead right. Promo 1: VO: 10” A pilot saved the day last Sunday on a Safair flight that suffered a gradual decompression over airspace in Bloemfontein. This time the passengers weren’t just clapping for a safe landing. Clapping Upsound “The pilots did their best” Promo 2: VO: 8 What happens during a decompression event at 32000ft – we bring you exclusive footage taken during a safair flight last Sunday. It’s not working? VO: 4” As long as your pilot knows what he’s doing it seems you are in safe hands. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Exclusive footage inside the cabin on Sunday night as a Safair flight experienced a loss of cabin pressure forcing the plane to drop 20000 feet in a matter of minutes.
metadata.Summary: We have 38 minutes of footage exclusive to us until after the show on Sunday night - shot by sports cameraman on board the SAfair flight from Johannesburg to Cape Town on Sunday night. About an hour into the flight the plane lost cabin pressure and the oxygen masks were manually dropped for the passengers. Some passengers in the footage reported that the masks did not work. Passengers panicked and say that communucation was scant and the airlines handling of the situation was terrible. Couple that with the fact that not only did the same airline have a problem 48 hours before with the same issue - it was the third incident of its kind in less than 8 months. It's brought maintenance and safety into question. Fortunately in all three instances the pilots handled the situations perfectly to avoid catastrophe. Cabin pressure is always carefully controlled and air disasters like the Helios plane crash in 2005 are largley due to pilot error. A small jet went down at the end of last year in Caledon killing the pilot due to a pressurisation issue. So its not commonplace but it does happen. What causes it and how should you react? And what are Safair doing to ensure their flights are safe?
